notes: Solomon is the foremost authority on Israelite wisdom (see 1 Kgs 3:1-28; 4:32). Many proverbs are ascribed to Solomon, but he did not write all of them (see Proverbs 22:17; Proverbs 24:23; Proverbs 25:1; Proverbs 30:1; Proverbs 31:1).

Wisdom is practical knowledge that involves ethical choices. Words such as right, just, and fair are associated with biblical wisdom. Gaining wisdom involves discipline, an active, intentional training of energy toward wisdom and away from folly. The book of Proverbs encourages us to resist our natural sinful tendencies toward wrong behavior.
This prologue explains the purpose of the book and identifies the different readers to whom it is addressed.
The simple are like empty containers. Wisdom and folly compete to fill their minds and hearts (see Proverbs 9:1-18).
Proverbs help the wise person to understand riddles. Here the Hebrew word (khidoth) indicates enigmas or paradoxes—difficult sayings that require interpretation (cp. Judges 14:14).

Fear of the Lord recognizes total dependence on God for everything, including knowledge and wisdom (Proverbs 9:10). It is not just a mental attitude but involves service, love, and obeying God’s laws (see Deuteronomy 10:12-13). Fear of the Lord is the basis of all knowledge. How can we understand life without knowing the most fundamental truth about it—that it is God’s creation?
There are two paths (Proverbs 1:15) in the book of Proverbs: a wise, just way and a foolish, evil way. The parents represent the wise way and encourage their child to follow it.

My child (Literally My son): Like other wisdom literature of the ancient Near East, much of chs Proverbs 1:1–9:18 is a father’s (and occasionally, a mother’s) instruction to a son. Because the son is being trained to follow in his father’s profession, much of the teaching concerns the son’s occupation. The NLT usually translates the term as child, since the lessons are applicable to both sons and daughters.
crown you . . . chain of honor: Ornaments often represent wisdom and its rewards (see also Proverbs 3:22; Proverbs 4:9). This imagery inspires readers to pursue wisdom with diligence.

The father warns his child not to join a gang of sinners in their plan to pounce on the innocent, for their evil actions will rebound on themselves (see Proverbs 28:10; Psalm 9:15; Psalm 35:8). The evil way is a path of violence and robbery.
like the grave: Hebrew like Sheol. In the Old Testament, Sheol is the abode of the dead. It is not necessarily associated with punishment.

Birds will not go into an obvious trap, but greedy people will. By resorting to violence and robbery, they will be violently robbed of life. They might be killed in the attempt or executed when caught. Even if sinners prosper until the end of their lives, they will find judgment in death, while the righteous will be in God’s presence (see Psalm 1:1-6).
The author personifies wisdom as a woman (the Hebrew noun translated wisdom, khokmah, is grammatically feminine) and encourages his son to embrace her (see Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 8:1–9:6).

Three main words in Proverbs describe those who lack God’s wisdom. Simpletons (Hebrew pethim) have not hardened themselves against God’s wisdom and are most open to correction (see Proverbs 1:4). Fools (Hebrew kesilim) have heard God’s wisdom but resist it. Mockers (Hebrew latsonim) not only resist wisdom but even ridicule it.

Wisdom invites all three groups (Proverbs 1:22) to come so she can make them wise. An intimate relationship with Wisdom means entering an intimate relationship with God, the foundation of true knowledge (Proverbs 1:7; see Job 28:1-28).
You ignored my advice—i.e., the call of God himself (see Psalm 14:1-7). God calls to us through creation (Psalm 8:1-9; Romans 1:18-20) and Scripture (2 Tim 3:16-17; 2 Pet 1:20-21).
I will not answer: If a person has not sought wisdom before calamity strikes, it is often too late to learn.
they hated knowledge: There is no middle ground in the language of Proverbs. One either loves and embraces Wisdom or hates and rejects her.
Evil people suffer the consequences of their own actions (see Proverbs 1:15-19); God will ensure that sinners receive their proper punishment (see Matthew 25:44-46; Hebrews 10:29; 2 Pet 2:9).
Truly wise people are untroubled by fear. They know that God is in control, and wisdom guides them in dealing with every situation.
To treasure my commands means to give attention to them and obey them; they allow us to live to the fullest.
The father urges his son to seek wisdom. It will protect him from evil men and from the dangers of promiscuous women. The son must seek wisdom, while understanding that it is a gift from God.
wisdom . . . insight . . . understanding: All three words point toward skills needed to navigate life’s difficulties.
Searching for silver or hidden treasures would be undertaken with urgency, excitement, and anticipation of reward (cp. Matthew 13:44; Luke 15:8-10).
The quest for true wisdom leads to God. Wisdom is impossible without fear of the Lord (Proverbs 1:7).
The Lord grants wisdom to those who learn it from the Scriptures, which come from his mouth (2 Tim 3:16; 2 Pet 1:20-21). It is impossible to become wise through empirical observation alone.
Here, common sense is intuitive understanding built through listening to God’s words and observing his world. God is a shield who guards and protects those who live in relationship with him.

Wisdom will enter your heart, becoming an integral part of life. Rather than occasionally doing wise things, the wise person consistently makes wise choices. • Knowledge brings joy because it helps people live successfully.

Wisdom discerns when words are twisted to represent what is wrong as being right. The right way leads to life, the wrong way to death (Proverbs 1:10-19; Proverbs 2:18-19; Proverbs 5:5-6; Proverbs 9:1-6, Proverbs 9:13-18). • dark paths: In the New Testament, darkness represents the realm of evil, while light represents the realm of God’s goodness (Matthew 4:16; Matthew 5:14-16; John 1:14; Romans 2:19).

Wisdom keeps a young man from an immoral woman, helping him to resist her flattering, seductive words. Wisdom includes emotional maturity, restraint, and the ability to assess the purpose of someone’s speech.
By pursuing another man, an immoral woman has abandoned her husband. Her marriage covenant . . . before God included vows of faithfulness (cp. Malachi 2:14-16).
leads . . . to the grave: Adultery betrays a fundamental covenant with one’s spouse and with God (see also Genesis 39:2-9; Malachi 2:14).

Those who make wise choices will live in the land; those who do not will be evicted. God gave the land of Israel to his people, but they could only stay in it if they followed God’s commands (Deuteronomy 28:9-11, Deuteronomy 28:64-68). Because they broke his law, they were expelled (in 586 BC; see 2 Kgs 25:1-30; 2 Chr 36:15-21).
To store God’s commands in your heart means not just memorizing them but making them an integral part of life and acting on them.
The Lord blesses those who trust him and seek his will. His correction benefits those who follow him.

Those who obey God’s laws are more likely to live many years; wickedness generally has negative physical and psychological consequences. However, evil people sometimes outlive righteous people (Ecclesiastes 7:15-18).
Loyalty and kindness reflect the intimate and wholehearted commitment of God’s covenant relationship with his people (see Deuteronomy 6:8-9). • Write them: For a parallel command, see Proverbs 7:3.
On the path of wisdom, God himself guides us by the wisdom embodied in his word.
Healing and strength mean enjoying physical vitality as God’s reward for following wisdom’s way.

God receives honor and blesses his people when they recognize him as the source of all they have and when they give him the best part of everything they produce (Genesis 4:3-5; Genesis 18:6; Numbers 18:12, Numbers 18:29).
The Lord’s discipline can take the form of hardships, disappointments, and frustrations (see Hebrews 12:4-6). Like a good father, God’s purpose is to make us wise, good, and happy.
Wisdom and understanding provide skill for living and handling life’s problems.
Wisdom is worth more than precious metals and jewels. It leads to relationship with God, the ultimate joy-giver (see Proverbs 2:1-8).
The tree of life alludes to the original tree in the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:9).
God’s wisdom created harmony in the universe. Having wisdom means living in conformity with principles embedded in creation.
This passage enumerates the benefits of common sense and discernment, which are fruits of wisdom.
A wise person is a kind and helpful neighbor. Proverbs strongly emphasizes helping the financially needy (Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14).
Because we have frequent contact with those who live nearby, we must not take advantage of them.
While it is impossible to avoid all conflict, we are not to pick a fight.

The violent will ultimately be punished for their ways (Proverbs 1:18-32), even if they seem to have an enviable position in the world (Proverbs 11:16). The wise will not envy them, because they are detestable to the Lord. God’s friendship is of far greater benefit than anything the violent achieve.

Discourses in chs Proverbs 1:1–9:18 often begin with the call to listen (cp. Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:23; Proverbs 2:1; Proverbs 4:20-21; Proverbs 5:1-2; Proverbs 6:20-23; Proverbs 7:1-3). • when your father corrects you: The children have reason to listen, because they have made mistakes.
Wise people navigate life’s difficulties successfully because they have heeded good guidance.
my father’s son . . . my mother’s only child: In Proverbs, both parents give instruction in wisdom. This involvement of both parents is unique among the traditions of the ancient Near East.

my commands: The words that describe the father’s teaching are used elsewhere in Scripture for God’s law. Fathers represent God to their children; the instruction of wise fathers conforms to God’s law.
In the Old Testament, to forget means more than not to remember; it is failure to obey.
she: In Proverbs, wisdom is sometimes personified as a woman (see Proverbs 1:20-33; Proverbs 8:1–9:6).
Wisdom often, though not always, brings relational and material prosperity.
A lovely wreath and a beautiful crown represent wisdom’s rewards (see also Proverbs 1:9 and Proverbs 3:22).

Not every wise person lives longer than every evil person, but obedience and wise living make a long, good life much more likely (see also Proverbs 5:1-14, Proverbs 5:21-23; Proverbs 23:29-35; cp. Ecclesiastes 2:12-17).
The father again lays two paths before his children, encouraging them to avoid evil with its horrible consequences and to embrace good with its promise of blessing.
Wisdom’s . . . paths are straight (nondeceptive), while those of a fool are crooked (Proverbs 2:15). • When you walk . . . run: The wise reach their goals more quickly and efficiently.
The wicked stay up at night to plan evil (Psalm 36:4; Micah 2:1).

To eat . . . wickedness and drink . . . violence means that those attributes are at the very center of someone’s life. Just as we eat and drink to stay alive, evil people sustain themselves by committing evil acts.

Light stands for wisdom and righteousness, and darkness stands for foolishness and wickedness (see Ecclesiastes 2:12-14). Light brings actions into the open; darkness hides them. Righteous people have nothing to hide, while the wicked try to hide what they do and end up stumbling over obstacles in the dark (see Matthew 4:16; Matthew 5:14-16; John 1:14; Romans 2:19).

pay attention: See also Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:23; Proverbs 2:1; Proverbs 5:1-2; Proverbs 7:1-3; Proverbs 8:1. The child is to let these teachings transform his personality, represented by his heart. A lifelong commitment to follow wisdom requires a change of heart.
The wise walk the path of life with eyes straight ahead.
Life and healing are rewards for following the wise instructions of the father (see Proverbs 4:10).

In the Old Testament, the heart represents the center of emotions, thinking, and reasoning (e.g., Genesis 6:5; Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 131:1). The heart is crucial in the battle between wisdom and foolishness, between righteousness and evil (see Matthew 5:8; Matthew 13:15; John 12:40; Romans 6:17).

Because a person’s words originate in the heart, Proverbs teaches extensively about speech. One of the most basic lessons is to avoid perverse or corrupt speech, later defined as lies, slander, gossip, and rumor (Proverbs 6:12; Proverbs 17:4; Proverbs 18:8).
Paying attention to instruction results in discernment—the ability to tell a right action from a wrong one. These instructions are vitally important when dealing with an immoral woman.

These instructions on embracing one’s wife and avoiding immoral women were originally addressed to young men just beginning their professional careers (see also Proverbs 2:16-22; Proverbs 7:1-27). This topic is also popular in ancient Egyptian wisdom writing.
The lips of the immoral woman seem sweet and enticing but are actually bitter and deadly. Sexual activity often begins with a kiss, and flattering words can entice.
A relationship with an immoral woman leads to death, as does a relationship with the woman named Folly (see Proverbs 9:13-18).

An illicit relationship can be tempting, but it eventually brings shame. If the woman is a prostitute, the young man will have to pay her and thus lose income. If the woman is another man’s wife, he might have to pay her husband (see Leviticus 20:10).

Some sexually transmitted diseases were well known in the ancient Near East. Leviticus 15:1-15 describes what is probably gonorrhea; other texts from Mesopotamia describe “the disease of intercourse” and the “disease of Ishtar” (goddess of love) with the physical symptoms of venereal diseases.

To drink from one’s own well (see also Song of Solomon 4:12, Song of Solomon 4:15) is to enjoy sexual relations within marriage. Rather than expend sexual energy on immoral women, a man should cultivate a healthy sexual relationship with his wife. Sex is not to be shared with strangers. This honors marriage (Genesis 2:22-25) and keeps the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18).
deer: cp. Song of Solomon 4:5.
Even if a man keeps an illicit relationship secret from his family and society, nothing is hidden from the Lord. Adultery is a sin against God (Genesis 39:8-9).
Habitual sins are like ropes that catch and hold people.
He will die: Young men must exercise self-control because death can result from acting on sexual desire for what is forbidden.

To secure the debt of another person is to guarantee it with one’s own possessions. Whether to earn a friend’s goodwill or to turn a profit from a stranger (cp. Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36-37; Deuteronomy 23:19-20), the risk is too great to take; it could lead to financial ruin. This message is repeated in Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 22:26; Proverbs 27:13.
save yourself: The danger of ruin is so great that escaping the situation is almost a matter of life and death, as highlighted by the images of animals caught in a trap.

Lazy people sleep rather than make necessary provisions (see also Proverbs 24:33-34). They are the opposite of self-motivated and industrious ants. • Extra sleep . . . more slumber sarcastically expresses a lazy person’s ambition.
// The result of laziness is poverty. It will come suddenly and ruthlessly, like a bandit or an armed robber.
eye . . . foot . . . fingers . . . hearts: The different parts of a worthless person’s body describe overall character, not just an occasional foolish act.
wink . . . nudge . . . wiggle: These behaviors were signals used while trying to deceive the innocent.
Even if wicked people seem to prosper, they will suddenly be punished.

The first line gives a number followed by a second line that increases that number by one. This device (called number parallelism) introduces a list of items and often, as here, draws attention to the climactic final item (see also Proverbs 30:15-23).
A false witness perverts the truth in court or in everyday conversation.
This passage emphasizes the life-threatening risk of sleeping with another man’s wife (see also Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:23; Proverbs 2:16-22; Proverbs 5:1-23; Proverbs 7:1-27).
The immoral woman uses smooth talk and physical beauty to appeal to the vanity of young men.
Sleeping with a prostitute has consequences, and sleeping with another man’s wife can cost you your life. Her husband will seek revenge (Proverbs 6:34-35), and God is watching in judgment.
walk on hot coals: Of course his feet will blister. The consequences are horrible.
Seven times is probably a way of saying a great amount since the law never stipulated such high repayment (see Exodus 22:1, Exodus 22:4, Exodus 22:9).

A thief might be punished severely even if he had a reason for his actions, but his punishment is nothing compared to an adulterer’s, who has no excuse for his crime. A jealous husband will seek the full punishment provided by law, which is death (Deuteronomy 22:22).
This is the last of four sections in chs Proverbs 1:1–9:18 that warn against the dangers of promiscuous women (see also Proverbs 2:16-22; Proverbs 5:1-23; Proverbs 6:20-35).
as you guard your own eyes: That is, with great care.

The Old Testament uses the phrase tie . . . on your fingers as a reminder for something that needs to be remembered, most notably God’s commands (Deuteronomy 6:8; Deuteronomy 11:18). • The NLT’s write them deep within your heart reflects the Hebrew idiom write them on the tablet of your heart (see also Proverbs 3:3). Only obedience that comes from the heart will last.
In Hebrew, sister is a term of endearment that expresses intimacy (see Song of Solomon 4:9-10).
Loving wisdom will leave no room for a promiscuous woman, whose arsenal includes flattery that appeals to a young man’s vanity.
Naive young men, not yet set in their ways, are still open to correction. With each foolish act, they move closer to becoming fools.
The young man’s father tells a story to illustrate his teaching about immoral women.
Foolish actions are often associated with darkness (see Proverbs 4:18-19; Ecclesiastes 2:13-14).
The woman, seductively dressed, looks good on the outside but inside is full of trouble.
Prostitutes commonly solicited business in public areas such as markets and at every corner of busy streets (e.g., Genesis 38:13-16).
The immoral woman’s observance of religious ritual makes her look good on the surface, but her immoral behavior reveals a corrupt heart.
Her emphasis on her bed and exotic perfumes (myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon) is explicitly sexual (cp. Song of Solomon 4:13-14).
let’s drink our fill of love: cp. Song of Solomon 5:1.
The naive young man’s foolish actions might cost him his life (see Proverbs 5:11; Proverbs 6:32-35).
The father reasserts the point of his lesson: While an adulteress might look good and a relationship with her is enticing, harm or even death will result.
Wisdom calls out openly and publicly, appealing to all and offering them her gift of wisdom. Like a prophet, she wants all to respond to her words.

The first part of Proverbs climaxes when the son encounters two women. Both invite the young man, and the reader with him, into an intimate relationship. The young man and the reader must decide between the woman named Wisdom, personifying the true wisdom of God (Proverbs 8:1–9:6), and the woman named Folly (Proverbs 9:13-18), representing the wisdom of the world (1 Cor 1:18–2:16). Both women’s houses are on “the heights overlooking the city” (Proverbs 9:3, Proverbs 9:14), suggesting ancient temples; the choice is thus between the true God and false gods.
The hilltop and crossroads provide maximum public access to all who pass by.

In ancient Near Eastern cities, the city gates had built-in chambers for conducting legal proceedings and business transactions. It was an appropriate place for Wisdom to make her appeal to the most people.

Wisdom is associated with truth, understanding, and knowledge, which are right, wholesome, plain, and clear. Wisdom detests deception, which is devious and crooked (cp. Proverbs 1:2-7; Proverbs 6:16-19).
Choose: An ethical choice must be made between seeking money or valuables and seeking wisdom, which is far more valuable.
Good judgment, knowledge, and discernment are only available to those who have Wisdom.
Those who choose wisdom, i.e., those who fear the Lord (see Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10), will not speak in ways that harm others or bend the truth.
The best rulers choose wisdom to guide them (e.g., 1 Kgs 3:16-28).

formed me from the beginning . . . I was appointed in ages past: God’s wisdom has always existed. His wisdom is here personified, but wisdom itself is not a person. Wisdom does not exist outside of God; wisdom is an expression of his character and nature. Unlike pagan gods, God needs no outside counselor to give him instructions (see Isaiah 40:13-14). Jesus is the apex of God’s wisdom (see Colossians 1:15-17; Colossians 2:3).
God used his wisdom to establish the created order, so wisdom can tell us how the world works and testifies to God’s greatness.
architect: God’s wisdom guided the shaping of creation, bringing order out of chaos.
Wisdom offers great rewards to those who listen to and follow wisdom.
Life is the ultimate reward for the wise, while rejecting wisdom results in death. These verses point to eternal life and death (see Luke 23:43; 1 Cor 15).
The number seven can denote grandeur or fullness, so the seven columns represent the grandeur of Wisdom’s house, the place where it dwells.
The invitation to join Wisdom for a lavish meal is met by a competing invitation in Proverbs 9:13-18.

In the ancient Near East, a great banquet would accompany a marriage, a military victory, or the making of a treaty. Wisdom’s celebration marks the beginning of a committed relationship with the hearer.
Throughout the ancient Near East, temples were built on the heights overlooking the city. A commitment to wisdom involves a commitment to the Lord (contrast Proverbs 9:14).

Wisdom makes her appeal especially to the simple and those who lack good judgment because they have not yet decided between wisdom and folly. See Proverbs 9:16, where Folly mimics and then perverts Wisdom’s words.
Wisdom gives people the ability to navigate life successfully.

These verses seem to create an awkward break between the invitations of Wisdom and Folly, but perhaps the purpose is to caution that, in contrast with inviting the simple (Proverbs 9:4), inviting mockers and the wicked is futile at best. Such people have already chosen their path and respond to Wisdom’s advice with violence. By contrast, the wise appreciate corrective advice; they welcome it and benefit from it.
Fear of the Lord: See study note on 1:7.
The woman named Folly is brash: Fools talk boldly and without shame but have nothing intelligent to say.
The woman named Folly also invites the simple and those who lack good judgment to join her for the banquet she has prepared. Her invitation and advice are antithetical to Wisdom’s (Proverbs 9:1-6).

On the heights overlooking the city was the traditional location for a temple. Folly personifies false gods and goddesses that compete for the affection and loyalty of God’s people (contrast Proverbs 9:2-3).
Like Wisdom, Folly has prepared a banquet for her guests (cp. Proverbs 9:2-5). However, this meal is dishonest and perverse.
Folly’s dinner guests end up in the depths of the grave, in contrast to the reward for Wisdom’s guests (see Proverbs 9:6).
The joy or grief of godly parents reflects the degree of their child’s obedience to principles of wisdom.

This long section is called The proverbs of Solomon. It consists mostly of brief bits of advice and observation. These sayings make heavy use of antithetical parallelism to contrast wisdom and righteousness with folly and wickedness. The arrangement of these proverbs appears to be essentially random, as in Egyptian and Mesopotamian wisdom literature. Some proverbs are repeated (see Proverbs 6:10-11 and Proverbs 24:33-34; Proverbs 14:12 and Proverbs 16:25; Proverbs 18:8 and Proverbs 26:22; Proverbs 19:24 and Proverbs 26:15; Proverbs 20:16 and Proverbs 27:13; Proverbs 21:9 and Proverbs 25:24; Proverbs 22:3 and Proverbs 27:12). Sometimes a group of proverbs shares a similar theme (e.g., Proverbs 16:1-11).
Tainted wealth . . . right living: The book of Proverbs promotes good behavior over having money (see also Proverbs 11:18; Proverbs 13:11, Proverbs 13:22).

This proverb can be misused if outward results are regarded as a barometer of godliness. Job’s three friends, for example, wrongly reasoned that Job must have sinned to earn his suffering (see Job 22:6-11).
Lazy people are foolish, while hard workers are wise (see also Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 26:13-16).
the name of a wicked person rots away: In ancient Israel, as is still true today in the Middle East, honor and shame were powerful motivators.
Paths are a metaphor for life (see Proverbs 1:15).

To wink at wrong suggests approving of bad behavior rather than confronting it. • but a bold reproof promotes peace: The NLT translators assume that the original text is reflected in the Greek version. The second line in the Hebrew text may have been copied by mistake from Proverbs 10:8.

As a fountain provides water that sustains life, the words of the godly give life to those who hear them. In contrast, the violent intentions concealed in the words of the wicked bring death (see also Proverbs 10:6; James 3:1-12).
beaten with a rod: People lacking sense will bring harm upon themselves through what they say. Concerning physical discipline, see Proverbs 23:13-14.
Although wealth can be a fortress against trouble, money can also create trouble (Proverbs 13:8) and can provide false security (Proverbs 18:10-11).
Wise people are not afraid to have their thinking or behavior corrected—they accept discipline as an opportunity to grow in wisdom.
Those who talk too much show their ignorance and get in trouble (see also Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 17:28).
Words are an expression of the heart.
The wicked might enjoy the material blessings of life, but only temporarily, in contrast with the godly. Jesus also expressed this reality (Matthew 7:24-27).
This proverb connects with God’s covenant promises to Israel (see Deuteronomy 28:1-14, Deuteronomy 28:63-68). Such connections are rare in the book of Proverbs.

Here, honest practices are applied to the business world (see also Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 20:10, Proverbs 20:23; Leviticus 19:35-37; Deuteronomy 25:13-15; Ezekiel 45:10; Hosea 12:7-8; Micah 6:11). • Scales were often made of two metal bowls suspended from a crossbar. The unit of currency, the shekel, comes from the verb meaning “to weigh” (see Amos 8:5-6).
Pride is dishonest self-promotion, whereas humility is an honest assessment of one’s strengths and weaknesses.

Right living, which flows from wisdom, is more important than riches. Nothing is wrong with riches (Proverbs 10:15, Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 14:24) that are gained properly (cp. Proverbs 13:11; Proverbs 21:6; Proverbs 22:16).
Our actions, whether godly or wicked, affect the whole city (cp. Ecclesiastes 8:9-13).
This perspective on a gossip is repeated in Proverbs 20:19.
The future of an entire nation depends on wisdom.
This message is repeated in Proverbs 6:1-5; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 22:26; Proverbs 27:13.
Respect is the great and lasting reward of being gracious, while wealth is the lesser and temporary prize of being ruthless (see also Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:18).
Godly behavior has positive consequences for the next generation.
Discretion is the ability to tell right from wrong, the beautiful from the ugly, and good taste from bad taste.
The wicked might prosper and the godly might suffer in the short term, but the future will right this imbalance.
Generous people who give freely to others will prosper, but those who hoard their money will lose it (see Proverbs 28:27; 2 Cor 9:6-9).
Money can be a blessing from God, but it is uncertain. The godly trust in God and flourish (see Psalm 1:1-6).
The implied answer is that wicked sinners will be punished on earth.

Elsewhere in Proverbs a crown symbolizes wealth (Proverbs 14:24), long life (Proverbs 16:31), and grandchildren (Proverbs 17:6). • cancer (literally rot): A disgraceful wife is a deep and life-threatening problem.
The wicked might prosper momentarily, but they do not last. The family of the godly stands firm for generations.
To be sensible means to act only after reflecting on the consequences. A warped mind acts on impulse.
Reality is more important than appearance.
This proverb is repeated but with a different conclusion in Proverbs 28:19.
The instability of thieves can produce violent behavior at any moment. By contrast, the godly are well rooted: Their relationships are stable even under duress.
Fools fail to realize what the wise know—that listening is the way to learn.
Keeping a level head allows a wise person to think clearly and avoid reactions that could cause a fight.
The message of this proverb is repeated in Proverbs 14:5.
A wise child accepts a parent’s discipline: Gaining wisdom requires discipline and correction.
Having control of the tongue demonstrates wisdom (see James 3:1-12).
Appearances do not always reflect reality.
Money can be a blessing or a curse (see Proverbs 3:9-10; Proverbs 21:6).
snuffed out: Cp. Proverbs 20:20; Proverbs 24:20.
Oral messages were the primary form of communication, so an unreliable messenger delivering the wrong message could incite all kinds of trouble.
We are influenced by those we associate with.
Hard work does not always bring prosperity (cp. Proverbs 10:4-6; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4) because injustice occurs in the world.

Punishment is sometimes necessary to motivate instruction. Discipline is a product of love, whereas refusal to discipline one’s child is a sign of laziness (see also Proverbs 19:18; Proverbs 23:13-14; Proverbs 29:17).
Building or tearing down the home is a metaphor for strengthening or weakening one’s family.
The path is a metaphor for life and conduct (see Proverbs 2:13, Proverbs 2:20; Proverbs 3:6; Proverbs 4:11; Proverbs 6:23). • fear the Lord: See Proverbs 1:7.
A fool’s word can be used against him.
It’s easy to keep a stable . . . clean if it is empty, but a farmer without an ox has no harvest.
Honest speech and lies both flow from deep within a person’s character. Cp. Proverbs 12:17.
The godly acknowledge their mistakes and sins, leading to change and reconciliation. Fools defend themselves by making fun of guilt.

No one can fully understand the emotions of another (cp. Psalm 103:14; Isaiah 63:9; Nahum 1:7; Romans 8:27). Bitterness and joy are at opposite ends of the emotional spectrum; this poetic device of referring to polar opposites (merism) covers the whole range in between.
Although a house is typically more stable than a tent, wickedness destroys and tears down, while godliness builds up (Proverbs 14:1).
// The right choice is not always the one that seems right on the surface (see Matthew 7:13-14).
A person’s outward demeanor might not reflect what is in the heart.
Backsliders foolishly act against what they know to be good and right and wise.
Short-tempered people do not anticipate consequences before expressing anger. Schemers reflect, but they, too, are hated because of the evil that they do.
are clothed with foolishness: One’s true nature and heart attitude will eventually show in one’s demeanor.
This proverb might commend moderation, having neither too little nor too much (Proverbs 30:7-9).
blessed are those who help the poor: See also Proverbs 3:27-28; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14.

This proverb states a general principle, even though fools sometimes have wealth (Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:18), and poverty is not always the result of foolishness (cp. Proverbs 13:23; Proverbs 16:8).
The well-being and growth of the people, not wealth or military victory, are the true signs of a king’s success.
Wise people can control their emotions and express them appropriately.
A peaceful heart has resolved its inner tensions. Freedom from jealousy is beneficial to physical health.

Wise people help the poor (cp. Proverbs 11:24-26; Proverbs 28:27; see Leviticus 19:9-10; Deuteronomy 15:11; Deuteronomy 24:10-15; Isaiah 3:14-15; Jeremiah 2:34; see also James 2:1-13). • insult their Maker: See also Proverbs 17:5.
Proverbs infrequently hints at life after death. Some scholars think this verse refers to God’s granting courage to face death with dignity and serenity.
A great nation is not defined by wealth, power, or military victories (Proverbs 14:28) but by godliness.
Moderating emotions and suiting them to the context helps others listen to what we say without reacting.
A wise teacher presents lessons in an attractive way. Crude belching describes the ugly teaching of a fool.
Knowing that thethe eyes of the Lord is watching everywhere is motivation for wise behavior.
Wisdom requires learning from correction.

God blesses the godly with wealth (Proverbs 10:22; cp. Proverbs 10:15 and Proverbs 14:24). The wicked may also gain wealth, but it will bring trouble rather than blessing (Proverbs 11:4, Proverbs 11:18; Proverbs 13:11; Proverbs 21:6; Proverbs 22:16).
God looks beyond the outward actions of sacrifice and prayers to see if they reflect the heart’s attitude (see also Proverbs 21:27; Psalm 40:6-8; Micah 6:6-8).

Death and Destruction (Hebrew Sheol and Abaddon) personify the destiny of the dead. Sheol is the abode of the dead; Abaddon is a synonym for Sheol that has an added implication of punishment. • God knows all secrets (see Psalm 139:1-12).
Mockers cannot become wise because they keep criticism at a distance (cp. Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10).
What people feel affects how they present themselves (cp. Proverbs 15:30).
Whether we enjoy knowledge or trash reveals whether we are on the path of wisdom or of folly.
Personality affects our outlook on life.
A healthy fear for the Lord counteracts inner turmoil and brings inner peace. • Better to have little: See also Proverbs 16:8.
This better than proverb shows the relative value of wealth. A substantial meal (steak) is good, but love is better.
Controlling one’s anger is a sign of wisdom (see also James 1:19-20).
A lazy person can find all kinds of obstacles (e.g., a path blocked with briers) to avoid work (see Proverbs 10:4, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11, Proverbs 12:14; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 14:4).
An individual might not think of all the angles of a problem; a wise person invites advice from many advisers.
A wise person avoids death by choosing the path of life.
The proud think that they are self-sufficient. Widows in the ancient Near East were just the opposite—completely vulnerable and without means of support or protection.
The heart behind prayers determines whether God hears them.
Just as how we feel affects our demeanor (see Proverbs 15:13), what we experience (such as another person’s cheerful look or good news) can affect how we feel.
Fear of the Lord fosters humility because proper regard for God counteracts our delusions of self-sufficiency.
Our own plans will come to fruition only if God allows (see also Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 16:33; James 4:13-16).
God’s moral evaluation is what counts (see Genesis 8:21; 1 Sam 13:14; 16:6-7; Luke 16:15). This proverb is repeated almost verbatim in Proverbs 21:2.
God must affirm our plans (Proverbs 16:1), so it makes sense to ask his help in accomplishing our goals (see James 4:13-16).
The wicked will have trouble in this life and in death. Nothing is outside of God’s control (see also Romans 9:10-24; 2 Pet 2:9).
God detests the proud, who refuse to commit their ways to the Lord (Proverbs 16:3) and mistakenly believe that they can accomplish their plans on their own (Proverbs 16:1).
God’s unfailing love and faithfulness are foundational in his covenant relationship with Israel (see Exodus 15:13; Exodus 34:6-7; Numbers 14:18-19; Deuteronomy 7:9-11).
Better to have little: See also Proverbs 15:16.
Divine wisdom refers to divinely inspired guidance that helps the king make judgments (e.g., 1 Kgs 3:28; see also Psalm 72:2).
This series of sayings reflects on the king, who represents God’s power on earth.
The message of this proverb is stated four times in the collection (cp. Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 20:10, Proverbs 20:23).
These proverbs presuppose a wise, godly king (see Isaiah 9:6-7). Many of Israel’s kings loved wrongdoing and hated truth (e.g., Ahab in 1 Kgs 21).
The king is powerful, so people are wise to avoid his anger and gain his favor.
Wisdom and good judgment may lead to wealth, but wealth cannot buy wisdom.
The pride of those who resist God and stubbornly rely on their own strength (Proverbs 16:5) is self-destructive and foolish because, apart from God’s help, no one has the resources required for life.
This proverb repeats Proverbs 14:12.
Scoundrels, a troublemaker, and violent people all disrupt relationships, creating trouble with their harmful actions.
Godly people grow in wisdom as they grow older, so their gray hair is a crown (cp. Proverbs 4:9; Proverbs 12:4; Proverbs 17:6).
Patience and self-control are far more valuable than brute force.
We may throw the dice: These dice were not for gambling but were a means commissioned by God to determine his will (Exodus 28:30; see also Joshua 14:2; 1 Sam 10:17-27; 14:40-43).
Wisdom is so much more important than privilege that if children act like fools, a wise servant will rise to prominence over the household.
The Lord’s refining fire (see Psalm 66:10; Jeremiah 9:7; Malachi 3:2-3) separates what is precious from the impurities in a person’s heart (cp. Proverbs 16:2; Proverbs 21:2; Proverbs 27:21).
Lies (Proverbs 6:16-19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 25:18), gossip (Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 18:8), and slander (Proverbs 10:18) distort reality for malicious purposes.
To make fun of what God created is to mock God.

Only those who have been blessed with a long life live to become grandparents, and the continuation of the family line is a sign of God’s blessing (see Genesis 12:1-3). • parents: Literally fathers. This proverb applies to both fathers and mothers.
Maintaining a good relationship with another person means forgiving rather than dwelling on faults.
The wise will listen to a mild rebuke and act on good advice. Even harsh correction (a hundred lashes) will not change a fool.
Rebellion flows from the inner character of evil people who defy the punishment that will follow.
This saying cautions those who try to teach fools. A fool caught in foolishness will react with anger and violence.

opening a floodgate: Once a quarrel starts, it is very difficult to stop it; a dispute should be avoided if at all possible (see Proverbs 10:12; Proverbs 15:18; Proverbs 16:28; Proverbs 20:3; Proverbs 22:10; Proverbs 26:21).
The essence of this message is repeated in Proverbs 6:1-5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 22:26; Proverbs 27:13.
high walls: Foolish confidence in the ability to win a fight emboldens people to engage in disastrous arguments.
Wisdom is not a natural quality but must be pursued. Sensible people persistently cultivate wisdom, but a fool’s eyes cannot stay focused.
Foolish children: This proverb is equally true of sons and daughters.
Words flow from one’s character as water bubbles up from the earth (see also Proverbs 10:20; Proverbs 12:23; Proverbs 16:23; cp. James 3:10-12).
// Rumors may be delicious to hear and repeat, but they are deadly.
In a troubled world, only the Lord can save. The rich might believe their wealth is a strong defense, but the power of money is limited (Proverbs 11:4; Proverbs 13:8).
Haughtiness cultivates pride. It leads to failure because it does not allow for change in the face of criticism. Humility learns from others and leads to the honor of success.
A spiritual or emotional problem (a crushed spirit) can be more trying than a physical one (sick body).
See “Bribes” Theme Note.
It is important to hear both sides of a dispute. Only fools jump to conclusions and rush to judgment; the wise take time to discern.
Flipping a coin (literally Casting lots): Casting lots was a valid way of seeking God’s will (Numbers 27:21; Joshua 18:6-10). The Lord determined how the lots would fall (Proverbs 16:33).
Life and death: The wise speak thoughtfully (Proverbs 10:19; Proverbs 11:12; Proverbs 12:23) because they know that what we say has consequences (Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 14:3).
God will punish the powerful who disparage the poor; wise people care for the needy (Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14).
Some people who present themselves as “friends” are not. The wise see beyond pretense, discerning a real friend from false friends by how they act in adverse circumstances.

It is better to be . . . honest, though poor, because wealth gained by dishonest means is short-lived (Proverbs 10:2) and will not preserve one from harm (Proverbs 11:4; see also Proverbs 15:16-17; Proverbs 16:8, Proverbs 16:16; Proverbs 17:1; Proverbs 22:1; Proverbs 28:6).
Rushing into things without understanding is dangerous.
Rather than acknowledge wrong choices and actions, fools blame the Lord.
God will make sure that liars are punished (see Proverbs 12:17, Proverbs 12:19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 19:9).
It is in our self-interest to acquire wisdom because understanding helps us prosper.
The reference to a false witness (see also Proverbs 19:5) reminds us of the ninth commandment (Exodus 20:16).
A lion’s roar is a frightening prelude to life-threatening violence (cp. Proverbs 20:2). Dew on the grass is soothing and contributes to growth (see Proverbs 16:14-15).

No choice for a son is more important than a good wife (cp. Proverbs 31:10-31); a poor choice brings agony (see Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 11:22; Proverbs 12:4; Proverbs 21:9, Proverbs 21:19; Proverbs 25:24; Proverbs 27:15-17). The wise man will look to the Lord to give an understanding wife.
Keeping God’s commandments (i.e., the law of Moses) protects one’s life (see Deuteronomy 28:15-68).

Growing in wisdom requires discipline for everyone, including children (see Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:31-32; Proverbs 17:10). The temporary grief that accompanies discipline is worth the protection from ruin.
// This proverb is a humorous comment on the foolishness of being lazy (see also Proverbs 10:4-6, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11, Proverbs 12:27; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9).
A mocker is beyond help (see study notes on 1:22; 21:11). A leader should still punish him because the simpleminded will learn a lesson.
See Exodus 20:12; Exodus 21:15, Exodus 21:17.

Too much alcohol clouds a person’s judgment. The Old Testament is not against drinking wine in moderation (Proverbs 3:10; Proverbs 9:5; Psalm 104:14-15), but it adamantly opposes excessive drinking (Proverbs 21:17; Proverbs 23:29-35; Proverbs 31:4-5).
Queen Esther was willing to rouse the king’s anger and risk her life (Esther 7:1-10).
True friends are reliable even in difficulties.
The king should be the epitome of wisdom and justice.

Wise people recognize their own weaknesses. Pride prohibits people from seeing their faults (Proverbs 6:17-18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 18:12; see also 1 Jn 1:8-10).
False weights and unequal measures: Merchants, for example, should not cheat their customers by using false weights to weigh out grain (cp. Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 20:23).
The ability to observe and learn from experience is a divine gift.
Laziness generally leads to poverty (see Proverbs 10:4-6, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9; Proverbs 19:15, Proverbs 19:24; Proverbs 20:4).
Sellers must see past a buyer’s words to avoid being cheated.

// A wise lender gets security or a deposit on a loan. A stranger was an Israelite unknown to a lender, who required security. Proverbs warns the wise to avoid borrowing altogether (see Proverbs 6:1-2). • The message of this proverb is repeated in Proverbs 6:1-5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 22:26.
This perspective on the gossip is repeated in Proverbs 11:13.
An inheritance gained early in life is likely to be spent long before death, leaving nothing to live on.
See also Romans 12:17-21.
The message of this proverb is presented in three other proverbs (cp. Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 20:10).
God’s role in guiding our steps is clear (see Proverbs 16:1, Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 16:33). We do not need to understand why things happen, but we should not lose hope, for God is in control.
Counting the cost is particularly important when making a promise to God (see Judges 11:29-40; Ecclesiastes 5:4-6).
A king represents God on earth, so he should support the godly and punish the wicked.
The Lord’s light penetrates the human spirit: God sees deep into people’s hearts (see Proverbs 16:2).

God’s unfailing love and faithfulness are closely connected to his covenant with his people (see Exodus 34:5-7; Deuteronomy 7:7-9). The king represents God on earth, so God will protect him (see 2 Sam 7).
Physical punishment cleanses away evil: See Proverbs 13:24; Proverbs 22:15; Proverbs 23:13-14.
A king was the most powerful individual in an ancient nation, and it seemed that he could do as he pleased. However, God directs the heart of the king.
This proverb is repeated almost verbatim in Proverbs 16:2.
God is not pleased with worship unless godly actions flow from a godly heart (see Psalm 40:6-8; Micah 6:6-8).
Demeanor (eyes), character (heart), and actions are all significant. God hates pride (see Proverbs 6:17-18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 18:12).
The crooked path of foolishness ends with death; the straight road of wisdom leads to life.

// A marriage that looks good on the outside (in a lovely home) is unrewarding if it is filled with quarrels (see also Proverbs 21:19; Proverbs 25:24; Proverbs 27:15-17; cp. Proverbs 11:22; Proverbs 12:4).
Evil people do not just act evil; they are evil. No appeal will persuade them to act otherwise.
The simpleminded learn by seeing a mocker punished (see Proverbs 1:22; Proverbs 19:25). The wise do not need the threat of punishment because they already desire wisdom.

The Righteous One: God sees what the wicked do in the privacy of their homes and will punish them for their sins. Alternatively, the Righteous One might refer to the insight of any righteous individual.
God is just, so he will reward the innocent and punish the wicked. No wonder the godly love justice while the wicked fear it.
Those who have common sense can avoid life’s dangers.
The expenses of wine and luxury prevent people from amassing their resources—they spend rather than save.
The wicked will fall prey to the traps they set for others (Proverbs 26:27; see also Proverbs 11:8).
It’s better to live alone: Cp. Proverbs 21:9; Proverbs 25:24.
See also Proverbs 3:9-10, Proverbs 3:15-16; Proverbs 10:15, Proverbs 10:16, Proverbs 10:22; Proverbs 14:24.

Righteousness and unfailing love are character traits associated with Israel’s covenant with God (see Exodus 34:5-7; Deuteronomy 7:9-11). The covenant promised life and honor to those who obeyed God’s law (Deuteronomy 28:1-14).
A wise military strategist can devise ways to defeat stronger forces. This makes wisdom superior to raw power (cp. Ecclesiastes 7:12; Ecclesiastes 9:13-18).
Mockers: See Proverbs 1:25-27; Proverbs 9:7-9. Also see study note on 1:22.
Generosity is a trait of the godly, while stinginess is characteristic of fools (Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14). Paradoxically, the more you give, the more you get (Proverbs 11:24).

Human wisdom is impotent if it stands against the Lord (see Proverbs 16:1, Proverbs 16:3, Proverbs 16:9, Proverbs 16:33). Similarly, military power (represented by the horse) is impotent without the Lord’s blessing.
A wise person will never compromise his reputation in pursuit of money.
Remembering that the Lord made them both helps prevent the exploitation of the poor.
// The theme of taking precautions is found in several proverbs (Proverbs 14:8, Proverbs 14:15; Proverbs 21:29).

Fear of the Lord (see Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10) goes hand in hand with humility. A humble person knows that he is not the center of the universe. Humility is more valuable than wealth (Proverbs 16:19; see also Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 18:12).
Living by deceit is dangerous; corrupt people never know when their treachery will be discovered or backfire.
This is a warning against being a borrower; other proverbs warn against guaranteeing others’ debts (Proverbs 6:1-2; Proverbs 20:16).
Even a wicked ruler wants advisers who have a pure heart—i.e., who are completely loyal—and who can communicate with gracious speech.
This proverb reminds the wise (those with knowledge) that the Lord is in control.

Of the many proverbs on laziness (Proverbs 10:4-6, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 14:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9; Proverbs 19:15, Proverbs 19:24; Proverbs 20:4, Proverbs 20:13; Proverbs 21:25; Proverbs 26:13), this is among the funniest. Lazy people will come up with any outlandish excuse for not working.
An immoral woman, using flattery and seduction, tries to trap a young man to commit sin.
Wisdom is learned, not inherited or innate. It takes discipline to change foolishness into wisdom.
A person . . . gets ahead by hard work, not by exploiting the poor or bribing the rich (cp. Proverbs 22:29).

As with the prologue that opens the book of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:2-7) and the introductions to the individual discourses (see Proverbs 1:8-9; Proverbs 2:1-11), this section begins with an encouragement to listen. This wisdom is more than good practical advice—its purpose is to inspire trust in the Lord.

This section is ascribed to a group called the wise. Who they were is unknown. There is a reference to thirty sayings (Proverbs 22:20), and the wisdom sayings that follow can be divided into thirty sections that are similar to an Egyptian composition called the Instruction of Amenemope, which is also divided into thirty chapters.

thirty sayings: Early scribes noticed that the Hebrew word for thirty has been written in an unusual form (shlshwm) rather than the usual form (shlyshym). All the early translations of the Old Testament (e.g., Greek Septuagint, Latin Vulgate, Syriac Peshitta) read it as thirty. Nonetheless, some prefer to translate the word as excellent sayings.

Saying 1: God defends the weak, including the poor. Those who are well off are responsible to be generous to the poor (Proverbs 11:24-26; Proverbs 21:13; Proverbs 22:9, Proverbs 22:16; Proverbs 28:27).
Saying 2: An angry . . . hot-tempered person is unable to control his emotions and expresses his anger at inappropriate times.
Saying 3: The message of this proverb is repeated in Proverbs 6:1-5; Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 17:18; Proverbs 20:16; Proverbs 27:13.
Saying 4: Property was marked by stones set up as boundary markers; it was a great offense to move these ancient markers of real estate (see also Proverbs 23:10; Deuteronomy 19:14).
Saying 5: Those who hone their skills and work hard will have the best jobs and work for the best people.
Saying 6: Many proverbs address young men in government service. A ruler’s rich fare might tempt a novice to overindulge through lack of self-control. But he will be vulnerable when sated.
Saying 7: Riches can be God’s blessing (Proverbs 3:9-10, Proverbs 3:15-16; Proverbs 10:22), but there are other things in life that are more important.
Saying 8: Proverbs puts a high premium on generosity (Proverbs 11:24-26; Proverbs 21:13; Proverbs 22:9).
Saying 9: Fools ignore advice (cp. Proverbs 9:7-12; Proverbs 10:18), so the wise do not waste their breath (see Matthew 7:6).

Saying 10: The wise avoid unfair business practices and illegitimate gains (see Proverbs 22:28), knowing that the Lord will judge wrongdoing. • Redeemer: The NLT is probably correct in capitalizing the word Redeemer and identifying him with God, although a human redeemer might be intended.
Saying 11: listen carefully: Learning is the way to improve (see Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:24, Proverbs 15:31-32; Proverbs 17:10; Proverbs 19:24).
Saying 12: See Proverbs 19:18; Proverbs 29:17.
Saying 13: A wise parent will rejoice in a wise child (see Proverbs 10:1).
Saying 14: Sometimes sinners prosper, but the wise will see that to fear the Lord is what ultimately rewards (see Proverbs 1:7).

Saying 15: Discipline is necessary for living a wise and balanced life. Overindulgence in drink (drunkards, see also Proverbs 23:29-35), food (gluttons, see also Proverbs 23:1-3), or sleep (see also Proverbs 10:5; Proverbs 19:15) results in poverty.

Saying 16: This saying is an exhortation to pursue the wisdom that a godly father and mother provide. Unlike other ancient Near East wisdom texts, Proverbs attributes wisdom to both father and mother (Proverbs 1:8; Proverbs 6:20).

Saying 17: Falling for a promiscuous woman is a trap, not a source of benefit. Proverbs repeatedly emphasizes avoiding sexual relations outside of marriage (see ch Proverbs 5:1-23; Proverbs 6:20-35; Proverbs 7:1-27).
Saying 18: This extended saying portrays the foolishness of the person who overindulges in alcohol (see Proverbs 20:1).
Saying 19: See Proverbs 1:8-19.
Saying 20: See Proverbs 14:11.
Saying 21: See Proverbs 21:22.
Saying 22: Rulers should be wise (see Proverbs 8:5-6).
Saying 23: Fools are alienated from the community because of their evil actions.
Saying 24: A wise person has self-control and strength under pressure (e.g., Daniel 1:8-16; Daniel 3:1-18).
Saying 25: The wise do what they can to prevent injustice and suffering (e.g., Job 29:12-17).
Saying 26: Both honey and wisdom are sweet. Wisdom improves the soul, enhancing opportunities for the future.
Saying 27: Those who are godly will not allow a setback to keep them down. • Seven times is symbolic for “many times.”
Saying 28: This saying leads to Jesus’ call to love our enemies (Matthew 5:43-48).
Saying 29: Don’t envy the apparent prosperity of the wicked (see Proverbs 24:1-2), because their success is fleeting. • snuffed out: Cp. Proverbs 13:9; Proverbs 20:20.
Saying 30: The king is associated with the Lord, reflecting his power and sovereignty on the earth (see 1 Sam 12; Psalm 2:1-12).
Saying 1: Truthfulness in rendering judgment is a hallmark of wisdom (see Proverbs 6:19; Proverbs 12:17; Proverbs 19:28; Proverbs 24:28-29; Proverbs 25:18).
This addendum to the thirty sayings of the wise (Proverbs 22:17–24:22) includes five further sayings.
Saying 2: A true friend does not cover up problems but honestly points out areas for improvement. A wise person welcomes the correction of a friend.
Saying 3: A wise person establishes a source of income before spending money on himself.
Saying 4: The truth should not be bent, not even for revenge (see Proverbs 6:19; Proverbs 12:17; Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 19:28; Proverbs 24:23-24; Proverbs 25:18).

Saying 5: Laziness and love for sleep lead to poverty (see Proverbs 10:4-5, Proverbs 10:26; Proverbs 12:11; Proverbs 13:4; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 18:9; Proverbs 19:15, Proverbs 19:24; Proverbs 20:4, Proverbs 20:13).
This proverb repeats Proverbs 6:10-11.
During the reign of King Hezekiah (728–686 BC), wise men (advisers) collected these proverbs of Solomon and added them to the collection.
This warning reminds young men entering royal service that some things cannot be understood, including the king’s sometimes mysterious reasoning (e.g., 2 Sam 11:14-25; 24:3).
As silver is ready for use once it is refined of impurities, the king’s court can do justice when wicked people are removed. A little bit of evil can spoil much good (Ecclesiastes 10:1).
To gain an audience with the king, a wise person will practice humility instead of pride (cp. Matthew 20:20-28).
Rash actions often result in shame.
See Proverbs 11:13; Proverbs 20:19.

Timely advice and valid criticism are precious, beautiful, and rare (see also Proverbs 15:23; Proverbs 26:7, Proverbs 26:9), and should be welcomed (see Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:24, Proverbs 15:31-32; Proverbs 17:10).
Snow would be a welcome relief in Israel’s hot, dry summers (cp. Proverbs 26:1); trustworthy messengers refresh their employer by enabling him or her to plan for the future.

In Israel, rain is rare. When rain does not follow the appearance of storm clouds, it is like the disappointment caused by someone who gives empty promises. Cp. Jude’s description of false teachers (Jude 1:12).

Honey in moderation is tasty and healthy (Proverbs 24:13-14); too much will cause vomiting. This principle can be applied to other areas of life; for example, it is good to visit your neighbors, but not too often.
Lying can have deadly consequences (see Proverbs 6:16-19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25).
Contrary to expectation, compassion toward an enemy is more effective than anger (see Romans 12:20).
This proverb repeats Proverbs 21:9.
A spring or fountain that yields fresh water gives life. When godly people allow the wicked to dominate them, what was life-giving becomes deadly.
The wise have self-control and cannot easily be dominated.
It is not fitting to give honor to fools.
Curses and blessings can have real effect (see Genesis 27:1-41; Genesis 48:8-9, Genesis 48:15-20; Numbers 6:23-27), but an undeserved curse has no effect.
A fool is like a dumb animal that can only be guided by brute force (see Proverbs 10:13; Proverbs 14:3).
Proverbs are often context sensitive. Whether or not to answer the foolish arguments of fools depends on what kind of fool and what kind of situation.
A fool might know a proverb but not be able to use it correctly. Cp. Proverbs 26:9.
A proverb misapplied by a fool might actually cause harm. Cp. Proverbs 26:7.
A fool or a bystander might easily be lazy (see Proverbs 10:4-6) or incompetent (see Proverbs 26:6-7). An employer should beware!
Even when foolishness brings terrible consequences, a fool persists in it (Proverbs 17:10; see also 2 Pet 2:22).
Fools have hope because they might recognize their folly and seek advice. However, those who think they are wise will remain ignorant.
The lazy person: See Proverbs 6:6-11; Proverbs 10:4-5; Proverbs 15:19; Proverbs 22:13.
This proverb repeats Proverbs 19:24.
The wise avoid getting involved in other people’s arguments (cp. Proverbs 26:21).

Lies are extremely dangerous because they lead people to act on false information. Liars cannot cover up later by claiming that they were only joking (see Proverbs 6:16-19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 25:18).
A gossip and a quarrelsome person are both like fuel to the fire of trouble and discord.
This proverb repeats Proverbs 18:8.
People sometimes hide evil attitudes and wicked intentions through flattery. In the end, the true hatred of smooth talkers will be exposed.
People usually receive the bad consequences they intend for others (see Proverbs 1:17-19).
We should plan (Proverbs 24:27), but our plans succeed only when God so wills (Proverbs 16:1, Proverbs 16:3, Proverbs 16:33; James 4:13-16). Only fools think that they control the future.
The Hebrew word translated praise comes from the same root as “brag” in Proverbs 27:1. Bragging (self-praise) is foolish.
Fools cause heavy . . . resentment by their foolish words and actions.
Anger can be dangerous but can be countered with a gentle answer (Proverbs 15:1). Jealousy is harder to resolve (Proverbs 6:34-35).
A rebuke improves life by correcting harmful behavior (Proverbs 13:1; Proverbs 14:6). Hidden, unexpressed love has no value.
Wounds from a . . . friend are from a loving rebuke (Proverbs 27:5). They are better than flattery (many kisses) from an enemy who intends to harm rather than help.
Even the best teaching (honey) will be refused if offered at the wrong time. The key to real learning is the receptivity of the student.
A person who forsakes his family and strays from home will more likely find trouble than whatever he was seeking (e.g., Luke 15:11-16).
Nothing is more encouraging than heartfelt counsel from an intimate friend (see also Proverbs 27:6).
In a crisis, one might need immediate assistance, so it is important to have friends close by and neighbors who can help.
Fairly or not, parents are evaluated by their children’s public behavior.

It is important to speak appropriately for the circumstances (cp. Proverbs 15:23).
A quarrelsome wife: Cp. Proverbs 19:13; Proverbs 21:9, Proverbs 21:19; Proverbs 25:24.
iron sharpens iron: Wisdom comes from interaction, often critical, with a good friend (see Proverbs 27:6, Proverbs 27:9).

An employer values loyal workers who protect their employer’s interests. Wise employers give their workers incentives to be loyal, such as allowing them to eat the fruit (see Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Cor 9:7-10; 1 Tim 5:17-18).
Death and Destruction: See study note on 15:11. • Human desire is never satisfied by money, power, or pleasure.
A person who avoids conceit in response to praise demonstrates purity of character (cp. Proverbs 17:3).
Foolishness is deeply ingrained in the character of a fool.
Agricultural property can provide food and clothing from generation to generation; these resources require continuous labor and attention or, like riches, they disappear.
The wicked experience God’s curse for breaking his covenant (see Leviticus 26:14-17, Leviticus 26:36-37).
Wise . . . leaders rule justly and effectively (Proverbs 8:15-16).
Without law, chaos results and the wicked flourish.
Evil people seek gain by breaking the law. Justice ensures that they are punished and the righteous are rewarded.
Virtue is more valuable than material wealth. This proverb is repeated with a slightly different conclusion in Proverbs 19:1.
their parents: This proverb applies to both fathers and mothers.

The law prohibited charging needy Israelites interest on loans (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36; Deuteronomy 23:19). The rich were instructed to lend generously to the poor (Proverbs 3:27-28; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14).
A person who ignores the law shows no fear of the Lord (Proverbs 1:7), the lawgiver. That person’s prayers are hypocritical—why should God listen to them?
When the wicked take charge: See also Proverbs 28:28.
The wise admit their mistakes and sins and pursue correction (see Psalm 32:1-5).
A wicked ruler will not help the poor because his rule is not just. Like a roaring lion or an attacking bear, he destroys their lives.

tormented conscience: See 1 Sam 25:31; Romans 2:15; Romans 13:5; cp. Hebrews 10:22. • Don’t protect him! Murder is such a serious offense that a fine could not replace the death penalty (see Numbers 35:32).
This proverb is repeated but with a different conclusion in Proverbs 12:11.
quick riches: Wealth must be earned ethically, or it will cause harm and will not last (see Proverbs 13:11, cp. Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:18; Proverbs 13:22; Proverbs 21:6).
Rendering a wrong verdict based on a bribe is evil (Proverbs 17:23; Proverbs 22:16).
The wise desire honest criticism of their faults so they can improve (Proverbs 10:17; Proverbs 13:1, Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:24, Proverbs 15:31-32).
Callous children who exploit their parents are wicked (see Exodus 20:12).
Those who are greedy fight to control circumstances so as to gain riches. Trusting the Lord allows the wise to face life calmly and, ironically, to experience prosperity.
The one who walks in wisdom listens to the advice of others; those who trust their own insight show themselves foolish.
When the wicked take charge: See also Proverbs 28:12.
A man’s wisdom affects his parents (Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 15:20; Proverbs 17:21). • Prostitutes cost money and a man’s wealth is rapidly wasted on them.
A just king looks out for the rights of others; a ruler who accepts bribes uses his office for personal gain (see also Proverbs 17:23; Proverbs 22:16; Proverbs 28:21).
Flattery is usually a trap to taking advantage of someone (Proverbs 7:21-22; Proverbs 26:23).
Wise people learn to control their emotions; they remain calm even under stress.
The oppressor should be motivated to treat the poor more humanely because God created them both (see also Proverbs 3:27; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7).
Wisdom is not instinctive—it must be taught.
The wise accept divine guidance from God’s law, the guide to his will.
In some instances of discipline, tangible consequences might need to accompany instructions.

You are sworn to tell the truth: See Leviticus 5:1.
Fearing people is a dangerous trap: See Proverbs 1:7; Luke 12:4-5.

This superscription probably refers to the whole of ch Proverbs 30:1-33. • Agur son of Jakeh: Apart from this reference, Agur and Jakeh are unknown. If “from Massa” is the correct reading, then Agur was a non-Israelite (the tribe of Massa is known from Assyrian texts).
Agur expresses his ignorance (cp. Psalm 73:22, where the psalmist calls himself a senseless animal). The first step toward wisdom is acknowledging what we do not know.

In contrast to Agur’s ignorance and powerlessness stands the strength and wisdom of God (cp. Psalm 18:30). This is good news to Agur, who understands that God is a shield to all who come to him for protection.

Agur requests two favors from God: that God will help him not to lie (cp. Proverbs 6:16-19; Proverbs 14:5, Proverbs 14:25; Proverbs 25:18; Proverbs 26:18-19) and that he not be given too much or too little. It is not sinful to be rich (Proverbs 3:9-10, Proverbs 3:15-16; Proverbs 10:15, Proverbs 10:22) or poor (Proverbs 3:27; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14), but Agur wisely wanted to avoid the pitfalls of both.

These verses summarize the character traits that wise people despise. Fools dishonor their parents (Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 20:20; Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16), deceive themselves (Proverbs 8:7), think they are pure when they are filthy (Proverbs 20:9), are proud (Proverbs 6:17-18; Proverbs 11:2; Proverbs 13:10; Proverbs 15:33; Proverbs 16:18; Proverbs 18:12; Proverbs 19:20; Proverbs 29:23), wound others with their words (teeth like swords, see Proverbs 25:18), and harm the poor (Proverbs 3:27; Proverbs 11:24; Proverbs 28:27; Proverbs 29:7, Proverbs 29:14).

The number parallelism (three . . . no, four) is a device for presenting a list of poetic examples. This list shows powers that are insatiable and often dangerous. See also Proverbs 30:18-19, Proverbs 30:21-23, Proverbs 30:29-31. • The grave, which stands for death itself, never seems to have enough—people keep dying (Proverbs 27:20). • barren womb: Women who are unable to have children often long to have them, like Sarah until she gave birth to Isaac, Rebekah until the birth of Esau and Jacob, and Hannah until the birth of Samuel. • The thirsty desert and a fire consume anything in their path.
People who are callous toward their parents will meet a violent end (see Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 19:26; Proverbs 28:24; Proverbs 29:3; Proverbs 30:11).
The writer stands amazed at how one thing moves on another.
The writer expresses horror at sex outside of marriage.

This proverb lists four things that make the earth tremble because they overturn the order of things. • who prospers (literally who is full of bread): In the ancient Near East as in much of the non-industrialized world today, having adequate food (bread) was a sign of prosperity.
Another example of number parallelism. Here, small, insignificant animals are surprisingly powerful and resourceful.

Lemuel, like Agur, might have been from Massa (see study note on 30:1). Lemuel’s mother’s teaching encourages him to control his lusts (particularly for women and alcohol) so that he might reign justly. • Apart from this passage, Lemuel is unknown.
The admonition not to waste energy on lust for women echoes earlier warnings (ch Proverbs 5:1-23; Proverbs 6:20-35; Proverbs 7:1-27).
Too much wine numbs the senses. A king needs his wits about him and should not overindulge in alcohol.
Rather than opening his mouth to drink wine (Proverbs 31:4-7), the king should speak up on behalf of the defenseless.
No one can find a virtuous and capable wife without God’s help (Proverbs 18:22). Such a woman, like wisdom, is more precious than rubies (cp. Proverbs 3:15).
Proverbs ends with a powerful poem celebrating the virtuous wife. The poem’s acrostic arrangement gives an impression of completeness and provides the student with an aid for learning.
This wife works to provide food and clothing for her family.
An excellent wife is engaged in commercial enterprises outside her home.
A virtuous wife is generous to the poor, another characteristic of wise people (Proverbs 11:24-26; Proverbs 21:13; Proverbs 22:9, Proverbs 22:16, Proverbs 22:22-23; Proverbs 28:27).
A capable wife’s industriousness enables her husband to distinguish himself among community leaders. In ancient Israel, civic leaders met at the city gates to conduct trials and make decisions.
The noble wife’s character exemplifies wisdom. She is coolheaded as she faces future uncertainties. She gives advice in a winsome way.
Those most important to the woman testify to her character, abilities, and achievements.
The book concludes where it began, by affirming the ultimate importance of the fear of the Lord (see Proverbs 1:7). A woman’s character is more important than her physical beauty.
